entry.title: What's Going Wrong with My JVM?! A Guide to First-Time Failure Diagnosis
entry.summary: It's 2 AM Friday night when you get alerts your primary business application stopped responding and user tickets are piling up. For situations like these, you need to have already captured the data that can help you quickly get a sense of what's going wrong. Yet many production environments don't have such data collection enabled, and some diagnostics have performance costs that are unsuitable for many production applications. In this session, we’ll use some commonly reported Java heap memory problems to show how to collect and analyze some low-cost data to diagnose those problems at first-time failure.

entry.title: Reflect, Transform, Accelerate: Bringing GPU Computing to Java
entry.summary: Java’s code reflection API, developed in OpenJDK Project Babylon, opens a new path to targeting foreign programming models directly from Java—including GPUs. This talk introduces the Heterogeneous Accelerator Toolkit (HAT), a Java parallel programming framework that accelerates modern workloads on specialised hardware through three core stages: reflect, transform, and accelerate. Through examples of tensor-core programming and matrix multiplication—fundamental building blocks for AI and natural-language processing—we demonstrate HAT in action. We also explore performance analysis and tuning of the CUDA backend with NVIDIA Nsight Compute and Nsight Systems, from profiling generated kernels to identifying optimisation opportunities.

entry.title: How Does Java Fit Into the World of AI—and How Can It Become an Even Better Fit?
entry.summary: In this video, we discuss why Java is already a good choice for AI and how existing and future Java platform features can make it even stronger. We explore developments across the language, libraries, and runtime, including OpenJDK Projects Amber, Babylon, Valhalla, and Panama, along with smaller improvements that can have a big impact when combined.

entry.title: Everyday JSON in Java
entry.summary: JSON is ubiquitous in modern software, and many use cases are just too small to justify adding external dependencies. To address these everyday use cases, a new JEP proposes a simple, incubating API for parsing, navigating, and generating JSON documents-both for Java developers and for the JDK itself. While the Java ecosystem offers many libraries with JSON-processing capabilities, this built-in API is not intended to replace them, but rather to offer a low-friction option when an external library would be unnecessary or impractical. In this talk, we will show how Data-Oriented Programming helps simplify the API, discuss its intended use cases, outline the design trade-offs, and demonstrate its capabilities.
